# Ticket

`customer_support.obj.core.ticket` · v1.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> One unit of promised work with a state, an owner and a clock. Those three things are the whole definition: if it has no state it is a note, if it has no owner it is a wish, and if it has no clock it is not a support ticket at all.
A Ticket is NOT the Conversation and it is NOT the Issue, and confusing it with either is the most common modelling failure in support software — every major ticketing product on the market has made at least one of the two. The Conversation is the message thread with the human; one conversation routinely spawns several tickets ("also, while I have you...") and one ticket can span several conversations across email, chat and phone. Collapse them and the second question is silently lost, which is why customers say they "already asked about this". The Issue is the underlying defect; hundreds of tickets can point at one issue. Collapse them and you can never answer "how many customers hit this", so the queue can tell you how busy it is but never what to fix. The tell that a system has made this mistake is that closing the ticket closes the bug, or that a merge destroys a requester.
A ticket can be closed while the issue behind it is wide open. That is not a bug in the model; it is exactly what "resolved" means when we shipped a workaround, and a model that cannot express it forces agents to keep tickets open to keep an engineer honest, which wrecks every duration metric in the queue.


Also called: `Case`, `Support Request`, `Incident Ticket`, `Work Item`, `Contact`

## States

Initial `new`

| State | Means | Entered when | Implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `new` | Arrived, unread, unowned. Every hour spent here is charged to the first-response clock and belongs to nobody. | — |  |
| `triaged` | Type, severity, priority and owner decided. Triage is complete when the ticket could be handed to a stranger without conversation — anything less is a queue with extra steps.  | — |  |
| `in_progress` | An assigned human is actively working it. The only state in which the queue is doing what it exists to do. | — |  |
| `waiting_on_customer` | We are blocked on the customer and the SLA clock is PAUSED. That pause is what makes this the most abused state in the queue: it is the only state an agent can enter unilaterally that stops the number they are measured on. The classic abuse is a question asked purely to trigger the pause, often one already answered earlier in the thread. Treat a ticket in this state whose last message asked nothing as a defect.  | `thread.ball_in_court = them` |  |
| `waiting_on_engineering` | Blocked on a fix we do not control. The clock keeps RUNNING, and it must — the customer did not choose our engineering backlog. Tickets die here quietly because nobody owns a queue they cannot influence.  | — |  |
| `resolved` | We believe it is fixed. An assertion by us, not a confirmation by them. Most systems treat this as the end and that is where reopens come from. Deliberately carries no `entered_when`: a quiet thread is not a fixed problem, and binding this state to ball_in_court = nobody because it is the nearest available predicate would silently resolve every ticket a customer gave up on.  | — |  |
| `verified` | The customer confirmed it. Rare, valuable, and the only honest input to a first-contact-resolution number. A queue with no verified state cannot tell a fixed problem from an abandoned one.  | — |  |
| `closed` | Terminal for this ticket. Says nothing about the issue behind it, which may be wide open. | — |  |
| `reopened` | The customer came back on the same problem. The truest quality signal support has, because unlike a survey it costs the customer effort. A reopen from `verified` is a far worse finding than a reopen from `resolved`.  | — |  |
| `escalated` | Ownership transferred upward or sideways WITH a named receiving owner and a reason. Not a synonym for urgent and not a synonym for the customer being angry — both can be true without this state, and an escalation with no receiving owner is a complaint wearing a workflow.  | — |  |
| `breached` | A promise was missed. A real state and not a flag, because what happens next differs: breach handling is its own motion with its own owner. Recording it as an attribute is how organisations discover their breach rate at quarter end.  | — |  |

## Constraints

- **`ticket.one_accountable_owner`** Exactly one assignee at a time. A queue is a waiting room, not an owner.
- **`ticket.clock_cannot_pause_on_us`** The SLA clock cannot be paused while we are the blocker.
- **`ticket.cannot_promise_beyond_entitlement`** No response or resolution commitment may exceed what the entitlement covers.
- **`ticket.cannot_close_with_reply_owed`** Cannot close while the observed ball is in our court.
- **`ticket.merge_preserves_both_requesters`** A merge may not orphan a requester or discard the merged ticket's clock.
- **`ticket.workaround_leaves_issue_open`** Resolving with a workaround cannot close the linked issue.
- **`ticket.escalation_needs_a_receiver`** Cannot enter the escalated state without a named receiving owner.
- **`ticket.severity_independent_of_account`** Severity may not be altered by account size. Priority may. Enforcing this is the only thing that keeps severity comparable across a queue. _(soft)_


## Business rules

- **`ticket.severity_is_not_priority`** Priority must not be derived from severity alone, and severity must not be raised because the account is large. They are separate decisions with separate inputs, and collapsing them is the single most expensive triage error there is.

- **`ticket.pause_requires_a_real_customer_dependency`** The SLA clock may not be paused while the thread says the ball is in our court. A pause entered when we are the blocker is a metric edit, not a state change.

- **`ticket.no_close_while_we_owe_a_reply`** A ticket must not be closed while the observed ball is in our court. Closing a ticket the customer is waiting on is the fastest way to manufacture a reopen and a detractor.
- **`ticket.entitlement_bounds_the_promise`** No response or resolution commitment may be made that exceeds what the entitlement covers. An agent promising four hours to a next-business-day account has created a breach that did not exist before they typed.

- **`ticket.exactly_one_owner`** A ticket in any state other than new has exactly one assignee. Two owners is zero owners, and a shared queue is not an owner.
- **`ticket.merge_never_destroys_a_requester`** Merging tickets links them and never deletes the merged one's requester or its clock. Two people who reported the same thing are two people owed an answer.

- **`ticket.missed_promise_is_a_breach_of_trust`** A commitment whose due time has passed with nothing sent outbound is a broken promise regardless of SLA state. Customers forgive slow far more readily than they forgive silence after a specific date was given.

- **`ticket.reopen_invalidates_verification`** A reopen sets verified_by_customer back to false and must not be counted as a first-contact resolution retrospectively.
- **`ticket.workaround_does_not_close_the_issue`** Resolving a ticket with resolution_type = workaround must leave the linked issue open. A queue that closes issues on workarounds looks healthy and ships the same fault to the next forty customers.

- **`ticket.escalation_requires_a_receiving_owner`** A ticket may not enter the escalated state without a named receiving owner. An escalation without one is a complaint and should be handled as one.


## Inputs

- **email** — who is waiting on whom
- **email** — last message from the customer
- **derived** — two-way volume against the prior fortnight
- **derived** — observation balance across the thread
- **derived** — correspondence tempo
- **email** — promises made in writing and their due dates
- **calendar** — support calls and their timing
- **ticket** — status, priority, severity, assignee, timestamps
- **chat** — live conversation and abandonment
- **phone** — call outcome and callback promises
- **survey** — CSAT, CES and NPS responses
- **crm** — account value, renewal date, plan
- **telemetry** — error rates and feature usage around the reported fault
- **status_page** — whether a known incident already explains this ticket


## Outputs

- **`triage_confidence_bp`** How sure we are the type, severity, priority and owner are right. Low confidence should route to a human, not to a queue. → L4.reasoning_unit, L4.decision_maker
- **`breach_risk_bp`** Likelihood this ticket breaches a promise before it resolves. Today derivable only from conversation shape, which makes it a rough prior rather than a forecast. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`blocked_on`** us | them | nobody | engineering. The one-word answer to 'why is this still open'. → L4.reasoning_unit, L5.execution_planning
- **`next_customer_update`** What the customer should be told next and by when, given what was already promised. → L5.communication_planning, L5.2.channel_planner
- **`escalation_candidacy`** Whether this ticket is escalation-shaped before anyone has declared one. → L4.decision_maker
- **`knowledge_gap_flag`** True when the ticket was answerable from content that did not exist. The input to deflection work. → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`cost_to_serve_signal`** Touches, reassignments and elapsed handling on this ticket, for the account-level aggregate. → L6.learning_unit


## Events

- **`ticket.opened`** Ticket Opened
- **`ticket.triaged`** Ticket Triaged
- **`ticket.first_response_sent`** First Response Sent
- **`ticket.paused_on_customer`** Clock Paused On Customer
- **`ticket.customer_waiting_too_long`** Customer Waiting Too Long
- **`ticket.promise_missed`** Promise Missed
- **`ticket.sentiment_turned`** Sentiment Turned Negative
- **`ticket.escalated`** Ticket Escalated
- **`ticket.breached`** SLA Breached
- **`ticket.resolved`** Ticket Resolved
- **`ticket.reopened`** Ticket Reopened
- **`ticket.closed`** Ticket Closed


## Actions

- **Triage the ticket** (human) — Set type, severity, priority and owner. Complete when a stranger could pick it up without asking anything.
- **Send a substantive acknowledgement** (agent) — A real first response, not an autoresponder. Stops the first-response clock honestly.
- **Verify entitlement before promising** (system) — Bounds what may be committed. Skipping it is how a breach is created at the moment of reassurance.
- **Ask the customer for what is missing** (agent) — Legitimately pauses the clock. Asking a question purely to trigger the pause is the abuse this action's audit trail exists to expose.
- **Chase a non-responding customer** (agent) — One chase before any close. The step auto-close is designed to skip, and the reason auto-closed tickets reopen.
- **Send a proactive status update** (agent) — Closes a broken promise before the customer has to chase. Cheapest available recovery of trust and the least-used move in support.
- **Reassign to another owner** (human) — Costs the customer a re-explanation every time. Track assignment_count, because the third reassignment is a triage failure and not a routing one.
- **Escalate with a named receiving owner** (human) — Transfers ownership with a reason. Without a named receiver this is a complaint and must not enter the escalated state.
- **Provide a workaround** (agent) — Stops the customer's pain and leaves the issue open. Both halves are required; doing only the first is how the same fault ships repeatedly.
- **Merge into another ticket** (human) — Links, never deletes. Both requesters keep their clocks and both get told.
- **Mark resolved** (agent) — An assertion by us. Not the end of the ticket and never the end of the issue.
- **Confirm with the customer, then close** (agent) — The step that separates a fixed problem from an abandoned one. Almost always skipped, which is where reopen rate comes from.
- **Reopen on the same problem** (system) — Resets verification and preserves the original clock history. A reopen that starts a fresh ticket hides the failure.


## Evidence

- **ticket** · 10000 bp — The system of record. Nothing outranks the ticket's own state — and nothing in this brain can read it today.
- **telemetry** · 9000 bp — Product data showing the fault occurring. The only source that can contradict both the customer and the agent and be right.
- **email** · 8000 bp — Written thread. Strong, timestamped, and the only source the pipeline actually has.
- **chat** · 7500 bp — Verbatim and timestamped, but routinely abandoned mid-sentence, so absence of a reply proves less here than in email.
- **survey** · 6500 bp — The customer's own verdict. Cheap for them to give, easy for us to time favourably, and biased toward the extremes.
- **phone** · 6000 bp — High-signal, badly evidenced. What was actually promised on the call survives only in whatever the agent typed afterwards.
- **crm** · 6000 bp — Account context. Someone typed it once and it has aged since.
- **status_page** · 5500 bp — Proves a known incident existed. Does not prove this customer was affected by it.
- **help_center** · 4000 bp — Article views before contact. Circumstantial, and the strongest available hint that content existed but did not land.
- **derived** · 4000 bp — Inferred from conversation shape. Corroborating only, never sole grounds for a state change.
- **manual_entry** · 3000 bp — An agent's own note. Honest, unverifiable, and written by the person being measured.


## Metrics

- **first_response_time** (hours) — Created to first substantive reply. Meaningless if autoresponders are counted, which is the default failure.
- **resolution_time** (hours) — Report it beside paused_minutes_total or do not report it. A clock-adjusted resolution time is a statement about our process, not the customer's wait.
- **wall_clock_wait** (hours) — Elapsed time ignoring pauses. The number the customer actually experienced.
- **reopen_rate** (percent) — The truest quality signal in support, because the customer has to act rather than merely feel.
- **sla_attainment** (percent) — Share of tickets meeting their promised clocks. Trivially inflated by pause abuse, which is why the next metric exists.
- **paused_time_share** (percent) — Share of ticket life spent paused. A queue whose paused share climbs while attainment holds is gaming the clock, not improving.
- **reassignment_rate** (percent) — Share of tickets that changed hands more than once. Measures triage quality, not agent quality.
- **touches_per_resolution** (count) — Agent replies per resolved ticket. The cost side of every deflection argument.
- **workaround_close_share** (percent) — Share of resolutions that suppressed a symptom rather than removed a fault. Rises quietly and predicts repeat contact.
- **verified_close_share** (percent) — Share of closures the customer actually confirmed. Usually embarrassing, and the honest denominator for first-contact resolution.


## Examples

- **Password reset via chat, resolved in four minutes** — A real ticket with a real clock. The argument for deflection is made entirely by tickets like this one, and the argument against auto-closing them is made by the ones where the reset did not work.
- **Sev1 outage on a free trial account** — Maximum severity, low priority. The inversion is correct and it is the thing triage most often gets wrong under pressure.
- **Sev3 UI defect on an account renewing in three weeks** — The mirror case. Low severity, high priority, and unavailable to the engine today because nothing commercial is visible on a support node.
- **One conversation that spawned three tickets** — 'Also, while I have you...' — the sentence that proves ticket and conversation are different objects. Systems that model them as one lose everything after the first question.
- **Four hundred tickets against one incident** — Answered once through the incident object rather than four hundred times. The moment where the ticket/issue distinction stops being pedantry and starts being staffing.
- **Closed on a workaround with the bug still open** — Correctly resolved and correctly unfixed at the same time. A model that cannot express this forces agents to hold tickets open to keep engineering honest, which wrecks every duration metric in the queue.
- **Paused for eleven days on 'awaiting customer'** — Resolved inside SLA. The customer had replied by phone. This is the ticket the pause-derivation pattern exists for.
- **Reopened twice after being marked verified** — Worse than a detractor survey. The customer confirmed it was fixed, then came back, twice — a diagnostic failure rather than a communication one.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **partial**


> Reference object for the Customer Support brain — copy this file's shape, and copy in particular the discipline that every pattern carries both a human statement and, where it can run, a machine `when`.
Eight of seventeen patterns are executable today. Not one of them reads a ticket field, because none exists in the substrate: they read thread.ball_in_court, thread.last_inbound, commitment.due_at, meeting.start_at, derived.sentiment, derived.engagement, derived.momentum and graph degree. The best of them — deriving the clock pause from the observed thread rather than from the agent's declaration — is genuinely useful and would be worth keeping even after a support pack ships, because it is an independent check on the field the queue most wants to manipulate.
The nine needs_signal patterns are ranked by what they would unlock. `ticket.status` is first and by a distance: the declared state of the central object of this domain is not projected into a typed fact, so the brain infers from email what the ticketing system knows for certain. `cancellation_threat` is second, because it is the moment support becomes a revenue question and it is stated in plain language in threads we already ingest. `ticket_reopened` is third, on the argument that it is the only quality signal a customer has to spend effort to send.
